import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Lovász–Plummer conjecture (proved 2011) and Sheehan's conjecture

*References:*
* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersen%27s_theorem#Related_conjectures)
* [LP86] Lovász, L. and Plummer, M. D. (1986). *Matching Theory.* North-Holland.
* [EKKKN11] Esperet, L., Kardoš, F., King, A. D., Král', D. and Norine, S. (2011).
  "Exponentially many perfect matchings in cubic graphs." *Adv. Math.* 227, pp. 1646--1664.
  [arXiv:1012.2878](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2878)
* [Sh77] Sheehan, J. (1977). "The multiplicity of Hamiltonian circuits in a graph." In *Recent
  Advances in Graph Theory*, Academia, Prague, pp. 477--480.
* [Th98] Thomassen, C. (1998). "Independent dominating sets and a second Hamiltonian cycle in
  regular graphs." *J. Combin. Theory Ser. B* 72, pp. 104--109.
-/

open SimpleGraph

namespace LovaszPlummerConjecture

variable {V : Type*}

/-- The number of perfect matchings of `G`. -/
noncomputable def perfectMatchingCount (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  {M : G.Subgraph | M.IsPerfectMatching}.ncard

/--
**The Lovász–Plummer conjecture (1970s), proved by Esperet, Kardoš, King, Král' and Norine
(2011).**

Every bridgeless cubic graph on $n$ vertices has exponentially many perfect matchings: there is
a constant $c > 0$ such that the number of perfect matchings is at least $2^{cn}$.
[EKKKN11] prove this with $2^{n/3656}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem lovasz_plummer_conjecture :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
      (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      (∀ v, G.degree v = 3) → G.IsBridgeless →
      (2 : ℝ) ^ (c * Fintype.card V) ≤ perfectMatchingCount G := by
  sorry

/--
**The explicit bound of Esperet–Kardoš–King–Král'–Norine (2011).**

Every bridgeless cubic graph on $n$ vertices has at least $2^{n/3656}$ perfect matchings.

*Reference:* [EKKKN11].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem lovasz_plummer_conjecture.variants.explicit
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hcubic : ∀ v, G.degree v = 3) (hbridgeless : G.IsBridgeless) :
    (2 : ℝ) ^ ((Fintype.card V : ℝ) / 3656) ≤ perfectMatchingCount G := by
  sorry

/-- A **Hamiltonian cycle** of `G`: a cycle passing through every vertex. -/
def IsHamiltonianCycle (G : SimpleGraph V) {v : V} (c : G.Walk v v) : Prop :=
  c.IsCycle ∧ ∀ w, w ∈ c.support

/--
**Sheehan's conjecture (1977).**

Every $4$-regular graph with a Hamiltonian cycle has a second Hamiltonian cycle (one with a
different edge set). Sheehan's conjecture would settle the last open case of the question,
raised by Smith's theorem for cubic graphs, of which regular Hamiltonian graphs have a second
Hamiltonian cycle: Thomassen [Th98] proved it for all $r$-regular graphs with $r \ge 300$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem sheehan_conjecture :
    ∀ {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      (∀ v, G.degree v = 4) →
      ∀ (v : V) (c : G.Walk v v), IsHamiltonianCycle G c →
        ∃ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), IsHamiltonianCycle G c' ∧
          c'.edges.toFinset ≠ c.edges.toFinset := by
  sorry

/--
**Thomassen (1998): regular graphs of large degree.**

Every $r$-regular Hamiltonian graph with $r \ge 300$ has a second Hamiltonian cycle.

*Reference:* [Th98].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem sheehan_conjecture.variants.thomassen
    {V : Type} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (r : ℕ) (hr : 300 ≤ r) (hreg : ∀ v, G.degree v = r)
    (v : V) (c : G.Walk v v) (hc : IsHamiltonianCycle G c) :
    ∃ (w : V) (c' : G.Walk w w), IsHamiltonianCycle G c' ∧
      c'.edges.toFinset ≠ c.edges.toFinset := by
  sorry

end LovaszPlummerConjecture

findings.description: The module reference labels Sheehan’s proceedings paper `[Sh77]` and dates it 1977 (lines 28–29); the `sheehan_conjecture` docstring repeats 1977 (line 79). The cited paper, “The multiplicity of Hamiltonian circuits in a graph,” was published in 1975. This is a bibliographic error, not a mathematical misformalization.
findings.source_evidence: Brinkmann–De Pauw, arXiv:2304.08946v6, bibliography, cites this paper in Recent Advances in Graph Theory (Proceedings of the Second Czechoslovak Symposium, Prague, 1974), pp. 477–480, 1975. Goedgebeur–Meersman–Zamfirescu, arXiv:1812.05650v2, §3.1.4 and bibliography, likewise cites the 1975 paper and distinguishes Sheehan’s different 1977 article, “Graphs with exactly one hamiltonian circuit.”
findings.suggested_fix: Change the reference to `[Sh75]`, with publication year 1975. Correct the theorem docstring’s date accordingly, or explicitly distinguish the 1974 presentation from the 1975 publication.

reformulations.difference: Perfect matchings are counted as subgraphs rather than as subsets of the graph’s edges.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A perfect-matching subgraph is spanning and has exactly one neighbor at every vertex. Its edge set therefore determines it uniquely, and every perfect-matching edge set gives such a subgraph. I proved equality with a computable enumeration of perfect-matching edge subsets in count_tests.lean. Finite V makes the set of subgraphs finite, so ncard’s infinite-set default is unreachable in the theorems.

reformulations.difference: The definition requires a cycle whose support contains every vertex, instead of explicitly requiring exactly one cyclic visit to each vertex.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Walk.IsCycle already prohibits repeated vertices after removing the initial occurrence of the basepoint. Consequently, covering all vertices gives exactly one visit per vertex around the cycle, with the usual repeated basepoint in the closed-walk representation. The equivalence with Mathlib’s Walk.IsHamiltonianCycle was proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: EKKKN’s displayed formulation includes the upper bound |M(G)| ≤ 2^|V(G)|; Lean states only the exponential lower bound.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The upper bound is unconditional for cubic graphs and is explicitly described as an elementary exercise in EKKKN. Repeatedly matching the first unmatched vertex gives at most three choices per pair of vertices, hence at most 3^(n/2) ≤ 2^n perfect matchings. Thus adjoining the upper bound does not change the conjecture.

reformulations.difference: Lean quantifies over simple graphs, whereas EKKKN explicitly allows loopless multigraphs for its main theorem.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The versions are equivalent with the same constant. In a cubic loopless multigraph, replace each double-edge pair by K4 minus an edge, attaching its two degree-two terminals to the original external edges. Both gadgets have two matching completions when neither external edge is used, one when both are used, and none when exactly one is used. Replace each isolated triple-edge component by K4; both have three perfect matchings. These replacements produce a simple bridgeless cubic graph, preserve the number of perfect matchings, and increase the vertex count. Its simple-graph lower bound therefore implies the original multigraph bound. The converse is restriction to simple graphs. This also applies to the existential-constant theorem. The local gadget counts were verified in Lean, but the complete graph-transformation equivalence was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: The source says that no 4-regular graph is uniquely Hamiltonian; Lean requires a second cycle for every given Hamiltonian closed walk, distinguishing cycles by undirected edge sets.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A graph with no Hamiltonian cycle satisfies both formulations vacuously. If it has one, the Lean condition supplies two distinct edge sets. Conversely, given two distinct Hamiltonian edge sets, at least one differs from any prescribed first cycle. Sym2 edges and toFinset correctly identify reversal and changes of starting point. The equivalence between the universal-first-cycle formulation and ‘if Hamiltonian, has two distinct cycles’ was proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Goedgebeur–Meersman–Zamfirescu summarizes Thomassen’s bound for even regular degrees at least 300; Lean includes odd degrees as well.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same source recalls Thomason’s parity theorem: in an all-odd-degree graph, every edge lies in an even number of Hamiltonian cycles. An edge of a given Hamiltonian cycle therefore belongs to another one. Thus the odd-degree cases are already known, and including them is equivalent to the cited even-degree result.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalization found in either definition or any of the four theorem statements. All status tags agree with the consulted literature. Lean checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, count_tests.lean, and hamiltonian_tests.lean compiled successfully without relying on sorry: they establish the empty-graph count 1, matching counts for small complete graphs, bridgelessness of K4, and two genuinely distinct Hamiltonian cycles in K5. Original LP86, Sheehan proceedings, and Thomassen full texts were not accessible; their claims were checked against explicit restatements and citations in the downloaded papers. The reviewed file’s hash matches the committed version; no checkout edits were made.
